[2024-03-22T09:06:00-07:00] HR’s finalist packet for Nadia is here.

From: HR
To: Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes
Cc: Sarah Kim
Date: Fri, Mar 22, 2024 8:41 AM PT
Subject: Nadia Singh finalist packet + proposed final loop

Morgan / Devon / Sarah —

Per the search calibration, sending the finalist packet for Nadia Singh inline below. She is the strongest fit we have seen for the actual brief: taking messy design-partner and early enterprise-adoption learning and turning it into a repeatable customer-growth motion, without treating roadmap exceptions as the job.

This is not a generic enterprise-sales VP readout. I’ve kept the interview notes in the same comparison frame we agreed to use for early calls, then pulled out reference themes and the proposed final topics that seem most worth probing.

-----------------------------------
CANDIDATE SNAPSHOT
-----------------------------------
Name: Nadia Singh
Current lane: customer-growth / enterprise-adoption leadership at growth-stage infrastructure/product companies
Relevant pattern match:
- has built post-design-partner onboarding and expansion motions before there was a mature sales org
- is comfortable with technical buyers, implementation friction, and early product gaps
- repeatedly frames customer trust as “clear boundaries + good follow-through,” not promise-making
- strongest when the company has signal but not yet a system

Why she rose to the top of the slate:
- Other strong candidates tended to drift into classic enterprise-sales language quickly (territory coverage, comp plans, pipeline mechanics, “what can product commit by quarter-end”). Nadia stayed anchored on activation evidence, adoption risk, expansion blockers, and operating handoffs.
- She appears genuinely comfortable in the in-between stage Scaffold is actually in: enough pull to matter, not enough structure to hide behind.

-----------------------------------
INTERVIEW NOTES
-----------------------------------

1) HR calibration screen
Date: Mar 11
Format: 45 min

Repeatable enterprise adoption
- Strongest section of the call.
- Nadia described her best work as turning “founder memory and scattered customer anecdotes” into a small set of repeatable stages, owner handoffs, and leading indicators.
- She asked early what design-partner learning currently lives in people’s heads vs. docs vs. product telemetry.
- She did not assume a big CS function, implementation team, or formal sales engineering layer already exists.

Judgment about not promising product
- Good boundary instinct.
- Said directly that early customer-growth leaders can do real damage if they confuse “earning trust” with “manufacturing certainty.”
- Her framing: if a feature is not committed internally, the external language has to stay at the level of current constraint, current workaround, and what evidence would change prioritization.
- She differentiated packaging/clarity work from true roadmap commitments without being evasive.

Ability to work without a mature sales org
- Comfortable with ambiguity and founder-heavy environments.
- She expects to draft playbooks herself at the beginning.
- Explicitly said she does not need a full RevOps stack to start; wants a reliable source of customer notes, activation milestones, and clear owner routing.
- Watchout: she has usually had at least one operations or program partner by the time the motion starts scaling.

Technical-buyer comfort
- High.
- Spoke fluently about technical evaluators, security/procurement drag, admin setup confusion, and where implementation friction masks as “customer hesitancy.”
- Did not oversell herself as a product manager, but seems able to hold her own with product and engineering leads.

Stage fit
- Good fit for the role as currently calibrated.
- She understands the difference between helping the company learn from enterprise-like customers and prematurely pretending the company is already a fully tooled enterprise vendor.
- Motivated by building the operating system, not inhe…

- Final-loop structure: 3 tightly run conversations, one shared scenario spine, same-day debrief.
  - Conversation 1 — 60 min, Morgan + Devon: Mercury activation, repeatable motion, and expansion failure modes.
  - Conversation 2 — 50 min, Devon + Sarah: Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals and owner handoffs.
  - Conversation 3 — 40 min, Morgan or HR: first-90-day build, stage fit, and support expectations.
  - Reserve 30 minutes immediately afterward for a structured debrief.

- Shared scenario spine:
  - “Scaffold has meaningful Mercury design-partner signal, but activation evidence is uneven and customer context is spread across founders and customer-facing teammates. Some accounts stall after initial enthusiasm.”
  - “At the same time, Evergreen-style customers are asking about SSO timing, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet.”
  - “Commercial framing has an owner, customer-thread continuity has an owner, and dates, quotes, and feature promises are not available before the relevant product work ships.”
  - Ask Nadia to state assumptions, identify the minimum evidence she needs, and distinguish messaging/package work, workaround work, process problems, and actual product gaps.

- Conversation 1 — Mercury activation and expansion:
  - Prompt: “Walk us through your first 30, 60, and 90 days to turn uneven Mercury activation learning into a repeatable customer-growth rhythm.”
  - Follow with: “Which failure modes would you investigate first—weak championing, admin friction, unclear value realization, setup trust, procurement drag, or poor handoff—and what evidence would distinguish them?”
  - Probe for:
    - A minimum viable evidence set rather than a large dashboard or new organization.
    - Clear activation stages, leading indicators, synthesis cadence, and owner routing.
    - A practical distinction between a product problem and a motion or onboarding problem.
    - Direct customer work where useful, without making customer-growth responsible for every customer-related issue.
  - Red flags:
    - Immediately proposing headcount, territories, quotas, or a conventional sales process.
    - Treating every stalled account as a product gap.
    - Using confidence or discounts to paper over weak activation evidence.

- Conversation 2 — Enterprise readiness and handoffs:
  - Prompt: “An Evergreen-like customer raises the four enterprise-readiness concerns above. How would you respond, learn from the pattern, and keep the conversation credible without creating bespoke roadmap commitments?”
  - Add a mixed-ownership example: “The request involves packaging clarity, a possible product gap, and customer education. Sketch the handoff between you, Sarah, Devon, and the product owner.”
  - Probe for:
    - What Nadia owns in the customer thread versus what Sarah retains.
    - When Devon should handle commercial or procurement framing.
    - How she records the request, classifies it, routes it, and closes the loop.
    - Language grounded in current constraints, available workarounds, and evidence that could change prioritization.
  - Red flags:
    - “We can probably make that work,” implied dates, informal exceptions, or roadmap negotiation.
    - Bypassing Sarah’s customer continuity or pulling Devon into every conversation.
    - Treating empathy and firm boundaries as mutually exclusive.

- Conversation 3 — First build, stage fit, and decision rule:
  - Ask: “What would you build yourself in quarter one, what would you deliberately not build, and what support or clarity would you need from Morgan, Sarah, Devon, and product?”
  - Ask: “What would tell you the motion is becoming repeatable rather than merely better documented?”
  - Score each dimension 1–4, using evidence from the scenarios:
    - Evidence-first prioritization.
    - Mercury activation and expansion diagnosis.
    - Enterprise-readiness judgment without product overcommitment.
    -…

- Head of Customer Growth - draft role description
- Reporting line: reports to Morgan Chen and works closely with Devon Hayes on commercial strategy, with Sarah Kim on active customer threads, and with product / engineering on enterprise asks.
- Why this role now
- Scaffold has moved from founder-led enterprise conversations into a period where it needs a single leader to turn early larger-customer interest into a scalable revenue engine.
- Mercury has created new pull from bigger customers, and we need someone who can land flagship accounts while helping define the go-to-market motion around them.
- This leader will bridge sales, customer success, solutions, and growth until dedicated functions exist.
- What the role owns
- Build the enterprise revenue motion from early pipeline through close, expansion, and renewal.
- Take over founder-led strategic accounts and personally drive marquee deals with senior buyers.
- Create account plans for top prospects and shape executive relationships with CIO, IT, security, and procurement stakeholders.
- Translate strategic customer asks into tailored solutions and coordinate with product / engineering on commitments needed to win or expand key accounts.
- Build repeatable packaging for security, procurement, pricing, onboarding, and executive follow-through.
- Partner with Devon Hayes on pricing and commercial structure, and with Sarah Kim on active enterprise customer threads.
- Stand up the first forecasting, pipeline review, and operating cadences for enterprise revenue.
- Help define when Scaffold should hire AEs, CSMs, solutions, or demand-gen support around the motion.
- First 6 months
- Close and expand a small set of high-value lighthouse accounts.
- Convert design-partner momentum into referenceable enterprise wins.
- Establish a 6- and 12-month revenue plan tied to top-of-funnel, pipeline coverage, conversion, and expansion targets.
- Build the first enterprise playbook for discovery, security review, procurement, rollout, and renewal.
- Identify the product gaps most likely to block large-account adoption and bring clear recommendations to leadership.
- Put basic sales systems and reporting in place so the company is not fully founder-dependent.
- Ideal background
- 8+ years in enterprise SaaS sales, growth, or GM leadership, ideally with experience at Series A through C scale.
- Experience closing six-figure to low seven-figure software deals with technical and security-sensitive customers.
- Comfort owning both individual deals and the management system around pipeline, forecast, and expansion.
- Ability to work cross-functionally with product and engineering and to push for customer commitments when needed.
- Strong executive presence with buyers, founders, and board-level audiences.
- Experience hiring and mentoring early sales or customer-facing teams is a plus.
- Candidate signals we want
- Has taken a technical product from founder-led selling to a more structured enterprise motion.
- Can talk concretely about security review, procurement friction, rollout sequencing, and post-sale expansion.
- Comfortable in ambiguous environments where the product and package are both still sharpening.

RECONSTRUCTED EARLY-CALL DEBRIEF TEMPLATE
2024 customer-growth / GTM leader search
Prepared: September 14, 2026

Purpose
Use the same comparison frame for every early call. The search is for a hands-on leader who can turn Mercury and Evergreen-like design-partner and early enterprise-adoption learning into a repeatable customer-growth motion. This is not a generic enterprise-sales VP search, and it is not authorization to trade bespoke product commitments for marquee logos.

Candidate: ______________________________
Interviewer: ____________________________
Call date / format: ______________________
Current company / role: _________________

Instructions for the debrief
- Capture observed evidence, not general executive-impression language.
- Separate what the candidate actually did from what they say they would do.
- Ask for the smallest evidence set, concrete owner handoffs, and the sequence of decisions.
- Record both strengths and watchouts; do not average away a material boundary failure.
- Compare candidates against this brief, not against one another’s charisma or brand-name employers.

Shared context to use in early calls
Scaffold has meaningful Mercury design-partner signal, but activation evidence is uneven and customer context is spread across founders and customer-facing teammates. Some accounts stall after initial enthusiasm. Evergreen-like customers are raising enterprise-readiness questions including SSO timing, admin-change audit history, clearer separation of admin and billing ownership, and a standalone procurement packet. Commercial/procurement framing has an owner, customer-thread continuity has an owner, and dates, quotes, and feature promises are not available before the relevant product work ships.

CORE COMPARISON CRITERIA

1. Repeatable customer-growth motion from messy evidence
What to test
- Can the candidate turn founder memory, scattered customer anecdotes, and design-partner learning into repeatable stages, use cases, proof points, owner handoffs, and leading indicators?
- Do they distinguish a real pattern from a single impressive account?
- Can they span discovery, qualification, security/procurement, rollout, adoption, expansion, renewal, and product learning without building process theater?

Evidence to capture
- A specific example of converting ambiguous customer signal into a repeatable motion.
- What inputs were reliable, what was uncertain, and how the candidate validated the pattern.
- The smallest useful operating cadence or system they built.

Rating (1–4): ____
Evidence / quote: ______________________________________________________
Watchout: _____________________________________________________________

2. Mercury activation and expansion diagnosis
What to test
- Can the candidate diagnose where accounts stall after initial enthusiasm?
- Do they distinguish weak championing, admin/setup friction, unclear value realization, setup trust, procurement drag, and poor handoff from a true product gap?
- Do they know which evidence to instrument first and what customer-growth should versus should not own?

Evidence to capture
- Proposed activation stages and leading indicators.
- A minimum viable evidence set, not a fantasy dashboard.
- How they would use direct customer work, internal synthesis, and owner routing.
- How they would tell whether a stalled account reflects a product problem, onboarding/motion problem, or commercial issue.

Rating (1–4): ____
Evidence / quote: ______________________________________________________
Watchout: _____________________________________________________________

3. Judgment about product truth and non-promising
What to test
- Can the candidate preserve customer trust without implying dates, quotes, security posture, exceptions, or feature commitments the company cannot support?
- Do they separate packaging/clarity work, workaround work, process problems, and actual product gaps?
- Do they treat customer requests as evidence to classify and prioritize—not as automatic roadmap input?

Evidence to capture
- A real example of declining or reframing a customer request without becoming evasive.
- Exact language they would use when a feature is not committed.
- What evidence could change prioritization and who would decide.

Rating (1–4): ____
Evidence / quote: ______________________________________________________
Watchout: _____________________________________________________________

4. Technical-, security-, and procurement-buyer comfort
What to test
- Can the candidate work credibly with technical evaluators, security teams, administrators, procurement, and executive buyers?
- Do they understand implementation time, source connection, sync/state trust, admin confusion, security review, and procurement drag?
- Can they discuss product details without pretending to be an engineer or product manager?

Evidence to capture
- Concrete technical or security-sensitive deal example.
- How the candidate separated buyer concern, current product fact, packaging issue, workaround, and product gap.
- How they kept the customer conversation moving without inventing certainty.

Rating (1–4): ____
Evidence / quote: ______________________________________________________
Watchout: _____________________________________________________________

5. Hands-on operation in an immature, founder-close organization
What to test
- Will the candidate personally build the first lightweight systems and cadence?
- Can they operate before a mature sales org, RevOps stack, CS function, implementation team, or sales-engineering layer exists?
- Can they reduce founder dependence without assuming every customer-facing problem belongs to them?

Evidence to capture
- What they would build themselves in the first 30/60/90 days.
- What they would deliberately not build in quarter one.
- Minimum support and clarity required from Morgan, Sarah, Devon, and Product/Engineering.
- Whether they have operated effectively with incomplete instrumentation and shifting ownership.

Rating (1–4): ____
Evidence / quote: ______________________________________________________
Watchout: _____________________________________________________________

6. Ownership and handoff discipline
What to test
- Can the candidate strengthen the existing owner split rather than bypass it?
- Do they understand that Sarah Kim retains live-account/customer-thread continuity and Devon Hayes owns commercial, procurement, and packaging framing?
- Can they classify, route, document, and close the loop on mixed requests involving customer education, packaging, process, and product?

Evidence to capture
- What the candidate would own in the customer thread versus what Sarah retains.
- When Devon should be pulled into commercial/procurement framing.
- How current product facts come from the appropriate product/engineering owners.
- Whether the candidate systematizes handoffs instead of taking over every account.

Rating (1–4): ____
Evidence / quote: ______________________________________________________
Watchout: _____________________________________________________________

7. Stage fit and repeatability orientation
What to test
- Does the candidate want to build an operating system from real signal, or inherit a large enterprise-sales machine?
- Do they understand the difference between learning from enterprise-like customers and claiming the company is already a fully tooled enterprise vendor?
- Can they sequence progress and reject deals that pull Scaffold away from a repeatable motion?

Evidence to capture
- What would tell them the motion is becoming repeatable rather than merely better documented.
- How they define success beyond signed enterprise ARR or a few large logos.
- Their comfort with a small number of well-fit accounts and explicit unresolved gaps.

Rating (1–4): ____
Evidence / quote: ______________________________________________________
Watchout: _____________________________________________________________

EARLY-CALL PROMPTS

Use enough prompts to get comparable evidence; do not run a broad sales-philosophy interview.

- “Tell me about a time you turned founder memory or scattered customer anecdotes into a repeatable customer-growth motion. What was the minimum evidence you needed?”
- “An account is enthusiastic initially but stalls. How would you distinguish weak championing, admin friction, unclear value realization, setup trust, procurement drag, poor handoff, and a true product gap?”
- “A technical buyer asks for SSO timing, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet. How would you respond credibly without creating bespoke roadmap commitments?”
- “What would you own in the customer thread, what would remain with the existing account owner, and when would you involve commercial/procurement leadership?”
- “What would you build yourself in the first 90 days? What would you deliberately not build?”
- “What would you measure to know customer growth is becoming repeatable?”

POSITIVE SIGNALS

- Concrete learning loops and clear separation of evidence from assumptions.
- Builds lightweight stages, definitions, cadence, and routing before requesting a large organization.
- Diagnoses adoption and expansion failure modes rather than labeling every stall a product problem.
- Comfortable with technical/security/procurement details and incomplete instrumentation.
- Protects product boundaries without rigidity; can give current constraints, available workarounds, and a credible path for learning.
- Personally builds systems, closes well-fit opportunities, and standardizes what works.
- Measures referenceable wins, qualified pipeline and conversion, shorter learning cycles, activation, adoption, expansion, and renewal—not only signed ARR.
- Works founder-close while making ownership explicit and reducing dependence over time.

WATCHOUTS / RED FLAGS

- Immediately reaches for territories, quotas, headcount, SDR/RevOps/CS structures, or conventional sales-process theater.
- Treats one lighthouse logo or one enterprise request as proof of repeatability.
- Treats every customer request as roadmap input or says “we can probably make that work.”
- Implies feature dates, security commitments, informal exceptions, discounts, or custom builds.
- Uses confidence to paper over weak activation or expansion evidence.
- Bypasses Sarah’s customer continuity, pulls Devon into every conversation, or assumes taking over externally means absorbing every internal decision.
- Requires a large support structure, avoids direct customer work, or is too managerial for the hands-on stage.
- Is uncomfortable with technical product detail or cannot own a full enterprise cycle through adoption and expansion.
- Frames the role as a generic VP Sales build-out or “close at all costs” mandate.

SCORING SUMMARY

Score each criterion 1–4 using evidence from the call.
1 = materially weak / no evidence
2 = partial or mostly theoretical evidence
3 = credible evidence with manageable gaps
4 = repeated, specific evidence strongly aligned to the brief

1. Repeatable motion from messy evidence:                 ____ / 4
2. Mercury activation and expansion diagnosis:            ____ / 4
3. Product-truth / non-promising judgment:                ____ / 4
4. Technical, security, procurement comfort:              ____ / 4
5. Hands-on immature-stage operation:                     ____ / 4
6. Ownership and handoff discipline:                      ____ / 4
7. Stage fit / repeatability orientation:                 ____ / 4
Total:                                                     ____ / 28

Decision recommendation
- Advance
- Advance with targeted probe
- Hold / compare after more evidence
- Do not advance

Recommendation: ______________________
Most compelling evidence: ______________________________________________
Biggest unresolved question: ___________________________________________
Required next probe: __________________________________________________

DECISION LIMITS

Advance only when the candidate demonstrates the four core capabilities across concrete examples or scenarios:
1. Builds from customer evidence into a repeatable motion.
2. Preserves product truth and does not broker bespoke roadmap exceptions.
3. Diagnoses activation and expansion failure modes with evidence.
4. Strengthens—not bypasses—the Sarah/Devon owner split.

Do not advance solely because of:
- Brand-name employers, impressive title, executive presence, or large historical ARR.
- One large logo, one successful deal, or generic claims about enterprise readiness.
- A polished pipeline/forecast answer that does not show adoption, expansion, or repeatability judgment.

Do not let the interview become:
- A territory, quota, pipeline-scale, or broad VP Sales screen.
- A “close this enterprise logo no matter what” exercise.
- Hypothetical feature-date negotiation.
- A debate about bespoke Evergreen/customer-specific commitments.
- A broad product-strategy assignment outside the current Mercury/customer-growth boundary.

Material boundary failures are disqualifying or require Morgan’s explicit review; do not average them away with strong selling credentials. If evidence is mixed, hold for a targeted scenario probe rather than filling gaps with assumptions. The final decision should be based on observed behavior, repeatability orientation, product-boundary judgment, and clean ownership—not charisma.

Debrief attendees: ______________________
Same-day debrief completed: Yes / No
Final notes: ___________________________________________________________

EARLY-CALL PROMPTS

Use enough prompts to get comparable evidence; do not run a broad sales-philosophy interview.

- “Tell me about a time you turned founder memory or scattered customer anecdotes into a repeatable customer-growth motion. What was the minimum evidence you needed?”
- “An account is enthusiastic initially but stalls. How would you distinguish weak championing, admin friction, unclear value realization, setup trust, procurement drag, poor handoff, and a true product gap?”
- “A technical buyer asks for SSO timing, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet. How would you respond credibly without creating bespoke roadmap commitments?”
- “What would you own in the customer thread, what would remain with the existing account owner, and when would you involve commercial/procurement leadership?”
- “What would you build yourself in the first 90 days? What would you deliberately not build?”
- “What would you measure to know customer growth is becoming repeatable?”

POSITIVE SIGNALS

- Concrete learning loops and clear separation of evidence from assumptions.
- Builds lightweight stages, definitions, cadence, and routing before requesting a large organization.
- Diagnoses adoption and expansion failure modes rather than labeling every stall a product problem.

- Protects product boundaries without rigidity; can give current constraints, available workarounds, and a credible path for learning.
- Personally builds systems, closes well-fit opportunities, and standardizes what works.
- Measures referenceable wins, qualified pipeline and conversion, shorter learning cycles, activation, adoption, expansion, and renewal—not only signed ARR.
- Works founder-close while making ownership explicit and reducing dependence over time.

WATCHOUTS / RED FLAGS

- Immediately reaches for territories, quotas, headcount, SDR/RevOps/CS structures, or conventional sales-process theater.
- Treats one lighthouse logo or one enterprise request as proof of repeatability.
- Treats every customer request as roadmap input or says “we can probably make that work.”
- Implies feature dates, security commitments, informal exceptions, discounts, or custom builds.
- Uses confidence to paper over weak activation or expansion evidence.
- Bypasses Sarah’s customer continuity, pulls Devon into every conversation, or assumes taking over externally means absorbing every internal decision.
- Requires a large support structure, avoids direct customer work, or is too managerial for the hands-on stage.
- Is uncomfortable with technical product detail or cannot own a full enterprise cycle through adoption and expansion.
- Frames the role as a generic VP Sales build-out or “close at all costs” mandate.

SCORING SUMMARY

Score each criterion 1–4 using evidence from the call.
1 = materially weak / no evidence
2 = partial or mostly theoretical evidence
3 = credible evidence with manageable gaps
4 = repeated, specific evidence strongly aligned to the brief

1. Repeatable motion from messy evidence:                 ____ / 4
2. Mercury activation and expansion diagnosis:            ____ / 4
3. Product-truth / non-promising judgment:                ____ / 4
4. Technical, security, procurement comfort:              ____ / 4
5. Hands-on immature-stage operation:                     ____ / 4
6. Ownership and handoff discipline:                      ____ / 4
7. Stage fit / repeatability orientation:                 ____ / 4
Total:                                                     ____ / 28

Decision recommendation
- Advance
- Advance with targeted probe
- Hold / compare after more evidence
- Do not advance

Recommendation: ______________________
Most compelling evidence: ______________________________________________
Biggest unresolved question: ___________________________________________
Required next probe: __________________________________________________

DECISION LIMITS

Advance only when the candidate demonstrates the four core capabilities across concrete examples or scenarios:
1. Builds from customer evidence into a repeatable motion.
2. Preserves product truth and does not broker bespoke roadmap exceptions.
3. Diagnoses activation and expansion failure modes with evidence.
4. Strengthens—not bypasses—the Sarah/Devon owner split.

Do not advance solely because of:
- Brand-name employers, impressive title, executive presence, or large historical ARR.
- One large logo, one successful deal, or generic claims about enterprise readiness.
- A polished pipeline/forecast answer that does not show adoption, expansion, or repeatability judgment.

Do not let the interview become:
- A territory, quota, pipeline-scale, or broad VP Sales screen.
- A “close this enterprise logo no matter what” exercise.
- Hypothetical feature-date negotiation.
- A debate about bespoke Evergreen/customer-specific commitments.
- A broad product-strategy assignment outside the current Mercury/customer-growth boundary.

Material boundary failures are disqualifying or require Morgan’s explicit review; do not average them away with strong selling credentials. If evidence is mixed, hold for a targeted scenario probe rather than filling gaps with assumptions. The final decision should be based on observed behavior, repeatability orientation, product-boundary judgment, and clean ownership—not charisma.

Debrief attendees: ______________________
Same-day debrief completed: Yes / No
Final notes: ___________________________________________________________

Date of record: September 14, 2026

Subject
What retention investigation Morgan wanted after the February 13, 2023 lead-partner meeting.

Executive finding
The meeting exposed a data-defensibility problem, not merely a presentation problem. Morgan wanted the retention analysis rebuilt from reconciled source data before presenting a definitive number: explain why Mixpanel and Devon’s CSV diverged, lock the cohort window and account-universe rules, and separate true retention from expansion effects and cohort/segmentation artifacts.

What triggered the investigation
- The lead partner asked two pointed retention questions. One answer was effectively hand-waved and the other was only partial, leaving Morgan concerned that the analysis had exposed a material weakness.
- The underlying figures already conflicted: Mixpanel and Devon’s CSV produced different results after sandbox and workshop accounts were excluded.
- The retention curve appeared to improve suspiciously quickly. Morgan suspected the cohort window might be creating the shape rather than a real product improvement.
- Morgan therefore did not want to keep polishing labels around a number that could not yet be defended.

Investigation requested
1. Reconcile the source data
   Compare Mixpanel, Devon’s CSV, and the underlying account-level records. Identify the exact point at which the figures diverge and document the query, export, filters, and calculation used for each cut.

2. Define the cohort and observation windows
   Test whether the apparent rapid improvement is caused by cohort-window selection, cohort maturity, or a changing population. Recalculate retention using a consistent, explicitly dated cohort definition and show which cohorts have enough elapsed time to support each month/week claim.

3. Establish the account universe
   State inclusion and exclusion rules explicitly, including sandbox, workshop, self-serve, throttled, and other non-comparable accounts. Quantify the effect of each exclusion rather than silently applying it.

4. Produce cohort-level retention cuts
   Replace the blended headline with one clean table containing explicit denominators. Show cohort-by-cohort logo retention and ARR retention, with the relevant month/week checkpoints and labels for immature cohorts.

5. Separate retention from expansion
   Provide an expansion-adjusted view so expansion does not mask churn. Show logo retention independently from ARR retention and make the numerator/denominator logic auditable.

6. Test for segmentation and instrumentation artifacts
   Check whether annual-plan transitions, seat expansion, self-serve reactivation, event mapping, or other instrumentation changes are distorting the curve. Distinguish genuine product improvement from a measurement or segmentation artifact.

7. Reassess the external claim
   Until the cuts reconcile, treat the number as directional rather than definitive. The external slide should state the methodology and caveat plainly, or omit a precise figure if the analysis cannot support one.

Requested output
- A reconciled, reproducible retention package.
- One clean cohort table with explicit denominators.
- Side-by-side source/sensitivity cuts showing the impact of account exclusions and cohort windows.
- Separate logo and ARR retention, including an expansion-adjusted view.
- A short list of unresolved data or instrumentation issues, with owners and next validation steps.

Historical follow-through
On February 14, Morgan asked Devon for the real month-12 retention cut rather than the blended view, including cohort-by-cohort logo and ARR retention, the effect of removing the 2021 self-serve wave, expansion-adjusted results that exposed churn masked by expansions, and one clean table with explicit denominators before revising the retention slide. Devon later took ownership of retention cleanup with Accounting and committed to cohort-by-cohort month-12 cuts, including a version excluding throttled accounts. The first signup-month cut arrived in March; it was considered potentially workable but still required validation for event mapping and possible self-serve reactivation miscounts.

Interpretation
The investigation was intended to answer a narrow but consequential question: is the improving retention shape real and repeatable, or is it produced by source disagreement, cohort-window choices, account exclusions, expansion masking, or instrumentation defects? Morgan’s desired standard was evidence that could survive partner scrutiny—not a cleaner-looking slide.

Historical scope
This note records the API v1 implementation from early April 2023. It is archival context only and must not be treated as current API guidance.

- April 6, 2023: API v1 was connected to the new billing setup. The billing integration wired the /charges and /refunds routes using the Basic Auth token created during the preceding sprint.
- April 8, 2023: POST /v1/webhooks was added for inbound events. It reused the API's existing Basic Auth setup rather than introducing a separate authentication approach, keeping the inbound-event route consistent with the rest of API v1.

Authentication note
For this historical v1 implementation, the billing routes and inbound-event route used the same Basic Auth model. This describes the system at that time; it is not a recommendation for new integrations.

Status and caution
API v1 was subsequently retired as part of the April 2023 migration to API v2, which used GraphQL with JWT authentication. Consult current API v2 documentation for present-day integration and authentication requirements; do not copy the v1 routes or Basic Auth behavior from this historical note into a new implementation.

input.body:
Archive note
Date recorded: 2026-09-14
Period covered: December 23, 2023 through January 1, 2024
Normal operations resumed: January 2, 2024

Subject
What new work product owners were allowed to receive during the reduced end-of-2023 holiday schedule.

Policy
The reduced holiday stretch was not an intake window for new product work. Product owners could receive only bounded closeout work in the two approved lanes:

- Mercury hardening follow-through.
- API v2 support cleanup.

A task was appropriate only when it could be closed using existing evidence, an available fix, or a tested update. The allowance covered follow-through on work already understood and actionable; it did not authorize new discovery, new commitments, or expansion of scope.

Deferred work
The following were to wait until January:

- New analysis or new data collection.
- Documentation sweeps.
- Migration rethinking or redesign.
- Non-customer-impacting polish and cleanup.
- Northstar packaging work, including screenshot refreshes, appendix wording, activation explanations, or support-pattern notes, as new product-owner asks.
- New customer roadmap or procurement commitments.

Operational boundary
Anything that was not customer-impacting should wait until January. During the coverage period, normal support rotation handled incoming issues, with named owners handling their existing technical, activation, commercial, or customer-thread lanes. Escalation was reserved for an actual incident, confirmed customer impact, or an unreachable documented escalation path. Non-urgent alerts and noise belonged in the Monday digest rather than becoming new holiday work.

Archive conclusion
Product owners were allowed to receive narrowly scoped, evidence-backed closeout items—not net-new product initiatives. January 2 was the restart point for substantive work, not a catch-up marathon.

input.body:
Date: 2026-09-14
Status: Historical handoff record
Scope: Mercury activation/onboarding UI and bounded design-partner launch, primarily the v0.2 operating model.

Purpose
This note records who owned the Mercury UI and release-readiness decisions, which artifacts were authoritative, and how disagreements were meant to be resolved. It is a historical handoff, not a reopening of settled design scope.

1. Ownership

Design and UX — Priya
- Priya was the single-threaded owner for activation and onboarding UX through launch.
- Her remit covered setup clarity, admin and invited-member handoff, failure-state legibility, recovery cues, and launch-critical copy and interaction decisions.
- Figma was the canonical source for design decisions and finalized strings.
- Marcus and Leo could identify usability or readiness risks, but they did not replace Priya as the final design decision owner.

Release readiness and dogfood gate — Marcus
- Marcus owned release-readiness and dogfood gating.
- The implementation checklist and release review were the canonical sources for readiness status; Figma comments were not the release gate.
- A flow could be held from shipment for unresolved behavior, missing evidence, or a launch-critical blocker even when its visual design was settled.

Technical release discipline — Leo Park
- Leo owned platform seams, release integrity, and architecture/system-trust risk as they affected Mercury.
- He evaluated edge-state behavior using repeated real dogfood evidence, distinguished proven behavior from demos or screenshots, and reported severity, seam risk, evidence, and remaining checks.
- Leo's technical assessment could block release on a real technical or system-trust risk, but polish alone was not a launch blocker.

Execution and evidence cadence — Jake
- Jake owned Mercury execution and the weekly launch-evidence path.
- MER-1279, the Mercury launch-readiness ledger, was the operating spine for blockers, evidence, decisions, and owner gaps.

2. Where decisions belonged

- User-visible flow, labels, helper text, state meaning, and interaction clarity belonged in Priya's design lane, with Figma as the source of truth.
- Implementation status, dogfood results, linked verification, and ship/no-ship readiness belonged in the checklist and release review, with Marcus as the gate owner.
- Platform seams, retry behavior, authentication or permission behavior, observability, and other system-trust risks belonged in Leo's technical review and in the linked evidence for MER-1279.
- Execution sequencing and evidence collection belonged in Jake's Mercury cadence and MER-1279.
- Scope changes, customer-facing promise limits, or decisions that exceeded the bounded launch belonged with Morgan rather than being smuggled into a UI polish decision.
- Later-scope enterprise-readiness work—such as SSO/SAML entry, audit history, or expanded admin-versus-billing-owner controls—was to remain outside the v0.2 review packet unless explicitly re-scoped.

3. Disagreement-resolution rule

1. Name the disagreement precisely: design intent, implementation behavior, technical seam, evidence gap, or scope/promise.
2. Put the issue in the authoritative artifact: update Figma for a design decision; update the checklist/release review and link proof for readiness; record the blocker and evidence in MER-1279 for launch tracking.
3. Let the owning function decide. Priya resolves UX intent; Marcus resolves the readiness gate; Leo resolves technical/system-trust risk; Jake keeps execution and evidence moving.
4. Do not reopen a settled design decision through scattered comments, pull requests, or chat. Reopen it only when user-visible behavior changes or there is real launch impact.
5. If a UX decision and readiness evidence conflict, keep the design owner and gate owner distinct: Priya decides what the intended experience is, while Marcus decides whether the implemented experience is ready to ship. Leo supplies the technical risk assessment where relevant.
6. Escalate only unresolved cross-functional conflicts or scope/promise changes to Morgan. The escalation should include the proposed decision, the authoritative artifact, evidence, impact, and one named final owner.

4. Historical release boundary

The bounded launch could proceed with the existing single-admin and magic-link model. MER-1746 (admin-setup labeling) and MER-1751 (retry-control guard) were treated as narrow, low-risk v0.2 work when their tests remained green. SSO, audit history, and deeper administrative controls were enterprise-readiness follow-ups, not reasons to expand the v0.2 UI handoff.

The practical rule was: settle UX in Figma, prove readiness in the checklist/release review and MER-1279, use Leo's evidence-backed technical assessment for seam risk, and keep scope decisions out of ad hoc UI debate.

Archive date: 2026-09-14

Subject: Leo Park’s approved involvement in the January 2025 Compass v0.1 work

Record

In January 2025, Leo’s approved role in Compass v0.1 was bounded technical involvement at the data and platform seams. With Jake, he could help test whether the renewal-risk/administrative-friction evidence and the post-first-live-sync expansion prompt were technically grounded, check event/source provenance and recency, and identify implementation or platform blockers. The January working session was to evaluate each signal by its triggered action, audience, evidence and caveat, account-note/source quality, and explicit non-goals—turning signals into owner-routed actions rather than a score or reporting artifact.

The work was deliberately narrow because Mercury activation was the January priority: workspace setup, first-source connection, first live sync, and teammate-invite/admin-role basics. Compass v0.1 was not approved as a general dashboard, customer-facing analytics surface, board dashboard, platform build, or new hiring lane. The project was intended to test what should happen when a signal appears, not to broaden product scope.

Return-to-Morgan boundary

Any request to move beyond seam validation and bounded prompt testing—especially dashboard or general-platform work, broader exposure, customer-facing claims, board/reporting framing, productization, or a new staffing lane—had to be brought back to Morgan for review before proceeding. Leo’s technical check could establish whether the seam was defensible; it did not authorize scope expansion or a conclusion that Compass had changed customer behavior.

Later clarification

The same boundary remained in force: Compass evidence required attached dates, sources, and caveats, and the work remained internal follow-up support rather than customer-facing proof.
